analysis.title: Regulation of Digital Assets in a Shifting Global Landscape
key_insights: Digital assets are moving from a stand-alone asset class into financial infrastructure. Regulation now shapes how money, securities and collateral move, and so affects currency use, capital flows, sanctions enforcement and market competitiveness.

Market size figures cited: cryptoassets about $3 trillion in market cap with a revenue pool of about $90 billion, stablecoins about $300 billion in circulation, tokenized real-world assets about $30 billion. In progressive scenarios tokenized real-world assets reach about 16% of global investable assets by 2035, around $88 trillion.

Institutional examples: BlackRock's BUIDL fund reached about $2.6 billion as of July 2026. DTCC has shown tokenized securities held in existing infrastructure used in digital market transactions. Hong Kong's digital green bonds apply tokenization across issuance, settlement and life-cycle management. Euroclear and Banque de France are migrating the €310 billion Negotiable European Commercial Paper market to DLT-based infrastructure.

The report sets out nine regulatory dimensions: perimeter and accountability, legal certainty, custody, infrastructure, digital money and settlement assets, monetary sovereignty and financial stability, prudential and collateral treatment, financial crime and sanctions, and market integrity and investor protection. The question shifts from whether a product is regulated to whether the surrounding system supports institutional use.

Across 35 jurisdictions and more than 25 activities, more than 70% regulate the activity rather than the legal form of the asset. Regulatory maturity is use case-specific. Switzerland has a framework for tokenized securities and DLT market infrastructure while its stablecoin rules are still being reformed.

Dollar-denominated stablecoins create a channel for digital dollarization. In markets with currency volatility or capital controls this can move usage away from domestic currencies and reduce authorities' oversight of monetary flows.

Stablecoins, tokenized deposits and tokenized money market funds make balances more mobile and rate-sensitive. Large-scale migration from deposits into fully reserved instruments could change bank funding and credit creation. Four transmission channels are named: collateral mobility, settlement architecture, bank funding and interest rate transmission.

Prudential treatment can decide whether tokenized assets are economical to hold or pledge. Recent US regulatory clarification treats eligible tokenized securities and their non-tokenized equivalents consistently, including for recognition as financial collateral. Liquidity metrics and stress tests need to cover continuous, off-hours markets.

In December 2025 CFTC staff gave conditional no-action relief allowing futures commission merchants to accept certain non-securities digital assets as customer margin collateral. The relief was reissued with a limited amendment in February 2026.

Financial crime control points are spreading across issuers, custodians, exchanges, wallet providers and network infrastructure. The Travel Rule is weaker for self-hosted wallets. Recent EU sanctions packages extend restrictions to cryptoasset service providers, decentralized trading platforms and specific digital currencies.

Market integrity: surveillance has to connect order-book, derivatives, decentralized protocol and on-chain data. Digital asset groups that combine venue, brokerage, custody, lending and market-making raise conflict-of-interest risk. Transaction ordering and oracle manipulation should be treated as misconduct by their economic effect.

Regulatory sequence differs by market. Markets with heavy retail trading need platform licensing first, markets with heavy foreign stablecoin use need reserve and monetary safeguards first, and tokenization-focused financial centres need legal certainty, custody and collateral treatment first.

Cross-border scale depends on trust in comparable regulatory outcomes, through recognition or equivalence calibrated by activity. Markets may integrate on asset issuance and distribution while keeping settlement, collateral, infrastructure and data tighter.

Business impact: friction-based revenue (slow settlement, fragmented records, closed distribution, manual intermediation, cross-border payment friction) is exposed. Value shifts to liquidity, risk bearing, trusted control, distribution and market access. Traditional institutions and digital-native firms will compete across the same parts of the value chain.
Shared infrastructure initiatives (Pontes, Appia, Project Agorá) shift differentiation from owning rails to connecting to and building on them.

Implementation priorities: common market standards, since firms can reach different conclusions on the same wallet or transaction. Coherence with legacy rules, such as the EU DLT Pilot Regime. Supervisors need to link on-chain data with traditional supervisory data, as in BIS and Bank of England Project Pyxtrial on stablecoin backing.

Appendix: only China keeps an explicit ban. Trading venues, custodians and payment providers are supervised in more than 75% of surveyed jurisdictions. Türkiye, Nigeria, Ghana and Argentina are moving to formal licensing. India has tightened AML registration. Bahrain, Kazakhstan and South Africa have licensed frameworks. Yield treatment on stablecoins remains inconsistent.

sector_views.rationale: Stablecoins may change deposit composition and funding costs. Banks can extend money, liquidity and balance sheet franchises into tokenized deposits, settlement and financing.
Regulated digital money pressures economics tied to payment friction, especially cross-border. Orchestrating across forms of money is a larger opportunity.
Higher standards erode advantages built on regulatory gaps and pressure integrated platform models. A larger regulated institutional market opens brokerage, financing and market making.

crypto_views: Cryptoassets are about $3 trillion in market cap and about $90 billion in revenue pool. Stablecoins are about $300 billion in circulation.
US efforts on the CLARITY Act reflect the need for a statutory framework for digital asset markets and clear responsibilities for financial regulators.
Stablecoin frameworks are formalizing quickly. Yield and reward treatment remains inconsistent across jurisdictions.
CFTC no-action relief lets futures commission merchants accept certain non-securities digital assets as customer margin collateral.
Entry of digital asset firms into banking, custody, brokerage and payments, and of traditional institutions into tokenized products, is blurring the line between the two sectors.
risk_factors: Fragmented regulation across jurisdictions and regulatory arbitrage across provider types.
Legal uncertainty over ownership, settlement finality and insolvency treatment of digital assets.
Dependence on foreign infrastructure and providers.
Continuous markets and off-hours outflows stressing liquidity, collateral and funding.
Distributed financial crime and sanctions control points, and weak Travel Rule coverage for self-hosted wallets.
Stablecoin-driven deposit migration affecting bank funding and credit creation.
Manipulation through transaction ordering and oracle inputs, and conflicts of interest in integrated platforms.
geopolitical: Digital asset regulation is tied to monetary sovereignty and control of critical financial infrastructure amid geopolitical fragmentation and a contested post-Bretton Woods order.
G20 has placed digital assets within discussions of financial modernization and cross-border coordination.
EU 20th sanctions package against Russia (April 2026) and 21st package (July 2026) reach energy, financial services and crypto.
Dollar stablecoins as digital dollarization in emerging markets, affecting capital flow management.

tension_points.bull_case: Tokenization and digital money can cut transaction and servicing costs, reduce settlement friction and make collateral use more efficient, which could justify migration from existing infrastructure.
tension_points.bear_case: Large-scale migration from deposits into fully reserved stablecoins and tokenized instruments could change bank funding and credit creation, and compress liquidity and crisis timelines.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Adoption stalls if digital formats do not improve outcomes enough to justify investors, issuers and participants changing established processes.

theme_stances.theme: digital asset regulation as financial infrastructure
theme_stances.key_argument: Regulation that resolves legal certainty, custody, prudential and settlement constraints lets digital assets work at institutional scale.
theme_stances.evidence: Digital asset regulation is now at the core of financial system design.

theme_stances.key_argument: Dollar stablecoins can accelerate digital dollarization and weaken authorities' oversight of monetary flows in currency-volatile markets.
theme_stances.evidence: Dollar-denominated stablecoins create a new channel for digital dollarization
